theme: 3 terms on literals: text written straight into code, the protocol that turns quoted text into your own type, and the protocol that does the same for square brackets

terms.definition: Text written directly in your code between double quotes, like "Mina".
terms.example: Move that String Literal into a constant, it's repeated in five places.
terms.code:
let name = "Mina"   // a string literal
let empty = ""      // also a literal
print(name.count, empty.isEmpty)

terms.definition: A protocol that lets a type be created straight from quoted text, by adding `init(stringLiteral:)`.
terms.example: Make `Endpoint` ExpressibleByStringLiteral, so we can write the path as plain text.

terms.definition: A protocol that lets a type be created from square brackets, like an array, by adding `init(arrayLiteral:)`.
terms.example: `Set` is ExpressibleByArrayLiteral, that's why the brackets work.

video.description:
Learn to explain literals in Swift: String Literal, ExpressibleByStringLiteral & ExpressibleByArrayLiteral, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
String Literal - Text written directly in your code between double quotes, like "Mina".
ExpressibleByStringLiteral - A protocol that lets a type be created straight from quoted text, by adding `init(stringLiteral:)`.
ExpressibleByArrayLiteral - A protocol that lets a type be created from square brackets, like an array, by adding `init(arrayLiteral:)`.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

landscape.hook: How can a plain string become your own type? Can you explain it in English?

dialogue.title: A string that isn't a String

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, `feed` is an `Endpoint`, but we assign it a plain string. How?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a String Literal. And `Endpoint` conforms to ExpressibleByStringLiteral.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So Swift calls that `init` for me?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. With ExpressibleByStringLiteral, any String Literal can become an `Endpoint`.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nice, that's much shorter to write.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And look at `ids`. It's a `Set`, but it uses square brackets.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: No. `Set` conforms to ExpressibleByArrayLiteral, so brackets can build it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So the duplicate 2 just disappears from `ids`?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Right. ExpressibleByArrayLiteral only builds the `Set`. The set rules still apply.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Got it. Quotes and brackets can build my own types too.
A String Literal is just text between quotes in your code.
